THE WORLD: CONTACT CENTRE AND CUSTOMER SERVICE
The first floor of a two-storey steel-framed customer service building from about 2012, on a business park at the edge of a coastal town: the contact centre of a regional energy and water supplier, about 220 seats in teams of 12 to 16. One deep open floor about 54 m long and 27 m across, 3.4 m from the raised floor to the white-painted ribbed steel deck above, with a long glazed wall facing north and, along the south side, a row of small glass-fronted rooms, the lockers, the kitchen and the stair core.
Architecture:
- the north wall is one long run of glazing: a grey aluminium curtain wall with slim mullions every 1.5 m, glass from a solid grey spandrel panel 0.9 m high up to about 3.0 m, one slim horizontal transom at 2.1 m (so each bay is a tall lower pane and a shorter upper pane), and outside each mullion a vertical aluminium fin 0.3 m deep; pale grey roller blinds, some lowered part way
- no suspended ceiling: the underside of the floor above is a white-painted profiled steel deck (shallow ribs about 0.3 m apart) on white steel beams at 3.4 m; below it, rows of felt acoustic baffles (upright blades 1.2 m long, 0.3 m deep, 4 cm thick, alternating marigold and pale grey) hang on fine wires with their lower edges at about 2.95 m; long linear LED lights hang between the baffle rows; a white sprinkler pipe runs above them with small pendant sprinkler heads
- square columns 0.45 m wide, cased and painted pale warm grey, on a 7.5 m grid: one line stands just inside the glazing, the others among the desks
- a raised access floor of 600 mm square panels (a 150 mm void for cables) under charcoal carpet tiles; bands of marigold carpet tiles mark the main aisles; a floor box with a hinged lid at each pod
- on the south side, small rooms with full-height clear glass fronts in slim grey aluminium frames and solid pale grey side walls; every glass front carries two frosted manifestation bands (plain, at about 0.9 m and 1.5 m); doors are light oak-veneer leaves in grey steel frames with a narrow vision panel
- desk pods of eight: sit-stand desks back to back in two rows of four, a marigold or slate felt spine screen along the middle, no side screens (neighbours sit 1.4 m apart), and wallboards hung from the deck above the aisle end of the pods
- in the north-east corner of the floor, the quiet room: a small room closed off by solid partitions, its outer side the north glazing with the blinds lowered; the coaching rooms are among the glass-fronted rooms on the south side; each team's huddle point is a clear patch of carpet against the west end wall, where a main aisle ends
Materials: charcoal carpet tiles with marigold aisle bands, pale warm grey walls and columns, white steel deck and beams, light oak veneer on desk tops and doors, grey powder-coated steel desk frames and monitor arms, felt in marigold (the company's colour: baffles, spine screens, one painted end wall) and slate grey, black and dark grey plastics for headsets and screens, a few green plants; signal red only on the few things that are red in life (a fire extinguisher, a fire alarm call point)

ORDER
1. Work ONE set at a time. For each: write its short plan (horizon y, vanishing points, focal point, light direction and
   shadow direction, free zones for characters with their anchors, what goes in far, mid and near), draw it, run the
   quality check, fix, save its file. Only then start the next set.
2. Never reuse one set's geometry, camera or furniture layout for another: each follows its own brief.
3. Do not draw any variants until I approve the main sets.

QUALITY CHECK (run it before you reply; redraw what fails and say what you changed)
Layout:
- Layout is cinematography: the camera height, angle and staging are decided before any rendering. Plan every set as far, mid and near ground, and leave clear space for the characters on the floor and around their heads, with breathing room on the side they will face.
- Prefer a low horizon (seated or standing eye height, never a high bird's-eye) so the room is not mostly empty floor and character sizes read clearly.
- Lead the eye with the architecture (a walkway, a table edge, a row of columns, the light pattern) to one focal point; the squint test must still show that focal point and the free space for the characters.
- Keep the backgrounds' values and patterns apart from where characters will stand: no busy pattern or high-contrast edge behind a head.
- Every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture rotated to the room gets its own vanishing points on the same horizon.
- Parallax: draw the walls and floor complete behind the furniture (no holes when layers slide), run the far layer past the frame edges into the overscan, and keep the near layer to one or two framing objects.
- Cast shadows and contact shadows on everything that touches a surface; without them objects look pasted in.
Real-world sense (nothing absurd):
- The horizon is the one in the camera line; furniture sits ON the floor with contact shadows; nothing floats,
  intersects a wall or passes through another object.
- Sizes agree with the scale list: chairs fit under tables, doors are taller than people, screens and windows are
  the stated sizes, steps and sills are reachable.
- The set was drawn, not modelled: soft things have curved edges, chairs have shaped backs and seats, and no shape is
  an unexplained slab or patch.
- Every object reads at a glance and in silhouette as what it is (a chair as a chair, a plant as a real plant);
  every object listed in the scene is present, and nothing is there that would not be in this place.
- Light has one logic: every cast shadow falls away from the named source at a consistent angle; screens and lamps
  glow only if they are on in this version.
- No people, no letters, numbers or logos; slots are empty rects; the palette is exact.
Not in this style:
- sketchy, choppy or wobbly lines
- every line the same weight
- corners that fall short of meeting
- heavy fills
- perspective errors (every receding line must meet its vanishing point)
Not in this world:
- a dark, windowless call centre or a science-fiction command deck
- a generic glass-tower office; exposed brick, small-paned steel factory windows, birch ply, brass lamps or deep green (they belong to another place)
- real brands, logos, signs with words, flags or anything that pins a country
- people in the sets (the cast is separate)
- words or numbers on wallboards, screens or papers (empty slots only)
- sun patches or hard sun shadows anywhere (the windows face north)
- screens facing a window or with a window directly behind them: screens sit at 90 degrees to the glazing
- a suspended tile ceiling or a low ceiling: the deck is at 3.4 m with baffles below it
- an agent headset drawn as music headphones: it has one or two flat ear pads on a thin band and a slim boom microphone
- a catalogue-clean floor: every scene shows that people work here
